title: Liver, gallbladder, pancreas and salivary glands
blurb: Know what each accessory organ makes, where its secretion goes and which hormone releases it.
question: A gallstone blocks the duct that carries bile from the gallbladder to the duodenum. Which step of fat digestion fails first, and which organ is still making bile?

teach.body: Formally, accessory digestive organs are structures that assist digestion but are not part of the alimentary canal: the teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas. In plain English: food never travels through them. The glands among them make secretions (saliva, bile, pancreatic juice) and pipe them into the canal through ducts, mostly into the mouth and the duodenum.

teach.caption: The three pairs of salivary glands are the parotid, submandibular and sublingual. Adults have 32 permanent teeth; children have 20 deciduous teeth.
Note the gallbladder tucked under the liver and the pancreas lying in the curve of the duodenum: bile and pancreatic juice both drain into the duodenum.

teach.h: The liver: the body's chemical plant
head: Liver job
Detail
rows: Iron; vitamins A, D and B12
teach.caption: The liver is the largest internal organ, in the right upper quadrant, and processes blood arriving from the gut in the hepatic portal vein.

teach.h: Bile emulsifies; it does not digest
teach.body: Bile contains no digestive enzyme. Its bile salts act like a detergent, breaking large fat globules into tiny droplets (emulsification). That greatly increases the surface area that pancreatic lipase can attack. So bile makes fat digestion possible and fast, but lipase does the actual chemical digestion into fatty acids and monoglycerides.

steps.sub: Stores and concentrates it between meals

teach.caption: Trypsin is released as inactive trypsinogen, then activated in the duodenum. These secretions come from the acinar (exocrine) cells.
A third hormone, gastrin, comes from the stomach and stimulates acid secretion.

teach.body: Keisha has a gallstone lodged in the duct that drains her gallbladder into the duodenum. After a fatty meal, CCK tells her gallbladder to contract, but bile cannot reach the duodenum. Her liver is still making bile; it simply cannot be delivered. Without bile salts, fat stays in large globules, so pancreatic lipase works slowly and fat digestion suffers. Starch and protein digestion carry on, because amylase, pepsin and trypsin do not depend on bile.

teach.text: Three classic swaps: the gallbladder STORES bile but the liver MAKES it; bile EMULSIFIES fat but lipase DIGESTS it; the pancreas secretes BICARBONATE (a base), not acid.

items: Salivary glands (parotid, submandibular, sublingual): saliva with salivary amylase.
Liver: bile, glycogen storage, detox, urea from ammonia, plasma proteins, vitamin and iron storage.
Gallbladder: stores and concentrates bile; contracts when CCK is released.
Pancreas exocrine: amylase, lipase, trypsinogen, nucleases, bicarbonate. Endocrine: insulin, glucagon.
Secretin releases pancreatic bicarbonate; CCK releases pancreatic enzymes and bile.

summary: You can now name each accessory organ, state exactly what it makes or stores, and follow bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum. You can also link secretin and CCK to their effects and avoid the classic bile, gallbladder and pancreas traps.

A.why: Liver cells make bile continuously; the gallbladder only stores and concentrates it.

whyNot.0: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile but does not make it.
whyNot.2: The pancreas makes pancreatic juice (enzymes and bicarbonate), not bile.
whyNot.3: The duodenum receives bile; it does not produce it.

A.q: Which component of pancreatic juice neutralizes the acidic chyme entering the duodenum?
A.why: Bicarbonate is a base, so it neutralizes stomach acid, protecting the duodenum and letting pancreatic enzymes work.

whyNot.1: Trypsinogen is an inactive protein-digesting enzyme; it does not change pH.
whyNot.2: Intrinsic factor comes from stomach parietal cells and is needed for vitamin B12 absorption.
whyNot.3: Pancreatic amylase digests carbohydrates; it does not neutralize acid.

A.q: Which statement about bile is correct?
options: It is an enzyme that breaks fats into fatty acids
It is made and stored by the gallbladder
It emulsifies fats so lipase can digest them
It enters the jejunum in response to secretin
A.why: Bile salts emulsify fat into small droplets, increasing the surface area on which pancreatic lipase works.

whyNot.0: Bile contains no enzyme; lipase is the enzyme that produces fatty acids.
whyNot.1: The liver makes bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it.
whyNot.3: Bile enters the duodenum, and CCK (not secretin) makes the gallbladder release it.

B.q: Which pairing of duodenal hormone and effect is correct?
B.why: Cholecystokinin (CCK) makes the gallbladder contract and the pancreas release its enzymes.

whyNot.0: Secretin's main target is the pancreas, which it stimulates to release bicarbonate.
whyNot.2: Gastrin is a stomach hormone that stimulates acid secretion; secretin triggers bicarbonate release.
whyNot.3: Secretin triggers bicarbonate release; enzyme release is driven by CCK.

B.q: Which is NOT a function of the liver?
B.why: Insulin and glucagon are made by the endocrine islets of the pancreas, not the liver.

whyNot.0: The liver converts toxic ammonia into urea, which the kidneys then excrete.
whyNot.1: The liver stores glycogen, iron and vitamins A, D and B12.
whyNot.2: The liver makes plasma proteins, including albumin and clotting factors such as fibrinogen.

B.q: Which substance is NOT a component of pancreatic juice?
B.why: Pepsinogen is secreted by chief cells in the stomach, where acid converts it to pepsin.

whyNot.0: Trypsinogen is a pancreatic protease precursor, activated to trypsin in the duodenum.
whyNot.1: Bicarbonate is the pancreatic base that neutralizes acid chyme.
whyNot.2: Nucleases in pancreatic juice digest nucleic acids.

C.q: Keisha has a gallstone blocking the duct between her gallbladder and duodenum. After a fatty meal, which process is most directly impaired?
options: Production of bile by the liver
Emulsification of fats in the duodenum
Protein digestion by pepsin in the stomach
Absorption of water in the colon
C.why: Bile cannot reach the duodenum, so fat is not emulsified into small droplets and lipase works far less effectively.

whyNot.0: The liver keeps making bile; the blockage stops its delivery, not its production.
whyNot.2: Pepsin works in the stomach, upstream of the bile duct, and does not depend on bile.
whyNot.3: Water absorption in the colon does not rely on bile delivery.

C.q: The pancreas is both an exocrine and an endocrine gland. Which pairing matches each role correctly?
options: Exocrine: insulin and glucagon; endocrine: lipase and trypsinogen
Exocrine: bile and bicarbonate; endocrine: insulin and glucagon
Exocrine: lipase and trypsinogen; endocrine: insulin and glucagon
Exocrine: lipase and pepsinogen; endocrine: insulin and gastrin
C.why: Exocrine acinar cells send enzymes (lipase, trypsinogen, amylase) through ducts; endocrine islets release insulin and glucagon into the blood.

whyNot.0: The roles are reversed: enzymes travel through ducts (exocrine), hormones go into blood (endocrine).
whyNot.1: Bile is made by the liver, not the pancreas.
whyNot.3: Pepsinogen comes from stomach chief cells and gastrin from the stomach, not the pancreas.

C.q: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, which liver action helps bring blood glucose back down?
C.why: The liver regulates blood glucose by taking up excess glucose and storing it as glycogen.

whyNot.1: Urea formation removes nitrogen waste; it does not lower blood glucose.
whyNot.2: Glucagon raises blood glucose, and it is made by the pancreas, not the liver.
whyNot.3: Albumin is a plasma protein; making it has no direct effect on blood glucose.

reteach.title: The kitchen and its cleaning supplies
reteach.question: Think of washing a greasy pan. Which supply breaks the grease into droplets, and which one actually dissolves it?

blocks.h: Soap, a bottle and a supply truck
blocks.body: The liver is the factory that makes dish soap (bile). The gallbladder is the squeeze bottle by the sink: it holds and concentrates the soap but makes none. Soap breaks grease into tiny droplets without destroying it; that is emulsification. The pancreas is the supply truck delivering the real cleaners (enzymes such as lipase) plus baking soda (bicarbonate) to neutralize acid. The salivary glands are the prep cooks who start on the starch.

blocks.text: Soap is not the cleaner that breaks the grease down chemically: bile emulsifies, lipase digests. And the bottle never makes soap: the gallbladder stores, the liver makes.

explain.body: Three pairs (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) release saliva into the mouth. Saliva contains salivary amylase, which starts starch digestion, and lingual lipase; it moistens food so the tongue can shape a bolus.

explain.caption: All three empty into the mouth.

test.q: Which enzyme in saliva begins the digestion of starch?
test.why: Salivary amylase starts breaking starch into smaller sugars in the mouth.

whyNot.1: Lingual lipase is in saliva but acts on fats, not starch.
whyNot.2: Maltase is a brush-border enzyme of the small intestine, not a salivary enzyme.
whyNot.3: Pepsin digests protein in the stomach.

explain.body: The largest internal organ. It makes bile, stores glycogen and regulates blood glucose, detoxifies drugs and alcohol, converts ammonia to urea, makes albumin and clotting factors, and stores iron and vitamins A, D and B12.

items.label: made here, not in the gallbladder

test.q: Which nitrogen-containing waste does the liver make from ammonia?
test.why: The liver converts toxic ammonia into urea, the main nitrogenous waste in urine.

whyNot.0: Uric acid is another urine waste, but it is not the product of the liver's ammonia conversion.
whyNot.1: Creatinine is excreted in urine, but it is not what the liver makes from ammonia.
whyNot.3: Bilirubin is a pigment (it causes jaundice when it builds up), not the product of ammonia.

explain.body: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile made by the liver. When chyme reaches the duodenum, CCK makes it contract and bile flows to the duodenum, where bile salts emulsify fat. Gallstones can block the bile duct.

test.q: What does the gallbladder do with bile?
test.why: The gallbladder stores bile made by the liver and concentrates it until CCK triggers release.

whyNot.0: Bile is produced by the liver, not the gallbladder.
whyNot.2: Bile contains no lipase; lipase comes separately from the pancreas.
whyNot.3: Bicarbonate comes from the pancreas and neutralizes stomach acid, not bile.

explain.body: Exocrine acinar cells make pancreatic juice: amylase (carbohydrates), lipase (fats), trypsinogen and chymotrypsin (proteins), nucleases (nucleic acids) and bicarbonate. Endocrine islets make insulin and glucagon. Secretin triggers bicarbonate; CCK triggers the enzymes.

test.why: Trypsin (from trypsinogen), with chymotrypsin, digests proteins in the small intestine.
